summary: Long-acting benzodiazepine used for severe anxiety, alcohol withdrawal, muscle spasm, and seizure emergencies. Carries high risks of dependence, withdrawal, and dangerous interactions with opioids and other sedatives.
description: Diazepam is a long-acting benzodiazepine that enhances the calming effects of GABA in the brain. In psychiatry and behavioral health settings, it is used short term for severe anxiety, to manage alcohol withdrawal, as a muscle relaxant in neurologic conditions, and as a rescue medicine for seizure clusters or status epilepticus. Because it is long-acting with active metabolites, diazepam can accumulate, especially in older adults, liver disease, or with frequent dosing. It has US boxed warnings for serious risks when combined with opioids, and for abuse, misuse, addiction, and withdrawal. For most chronic anxiety disorders, diazepam is considered a second-line or temporary bridge treatment rather than a long-term solution.
patient_summary: Diazepam (Valium) is a benzodiazepine that calms the nervous system. It can quickly reduce severe anxiety, help with alcohol withdrawal symptoms, relax tight muscles, and stop certain types of seizures or seizure clusters. Because it is long-acting, it can build up in the body over time. Diazepam can be habit-forming and is not meant for long-term daily use for anxiety in most people. Stopping suddenly after regular use can cause serious withdrawal symptoms, including seizures. Combining diazepam with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives can slow breathing and may be life-threatening.

primary.condition_name: Severe acute anxiety or agitation (short-term use)

secondary.context: Used short term for severe anxiety while first-line treatments (SSRIs/SNRIs and psychotherapy) are initiated and titrated. Not recommended as long-term monotherapy.
Common first-line benzodiazepine for moderate-to-severe alcohol withdrawal due to long half-life and anticonvulsant properties.
Rectal gel, intranasal spray, and buccal film formulations are used as intermittent rescue medications for seizure clusters in patients with established epilepsy.
IV diazepam is an accepted option for first-line treatment of convulsive status epilepticus when IV access and formulation are available.
Used as an adjunct for muscle spasm and spasticity associated with neurologic conditions (eg, cerebral palsy, spinal cord injury), typically when other agents are insufficient.
Generally avoided or used only briefly in PTSD because benzodiazepines may worsen cognitive processing and interfere with trauma-focused therapies.

therapeutic_response.display: IV: 1–3 minutes; rectal: 2–10 minutes; intranasal/buccal: within minutes; oral: usually within 30–60 minutes depending on formulation and food.

common_adverse_effects.notes: Often strongest early in treatment or after dose increases; can impair driving and daily functioning.
Increases fall risk, particularly in older adults or those on other sedatives.
May notice slower thinking, difficulty learning new information, or forgetting conversations and events.

serious_risks.risk: Respiratory depression, especially with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives
Severe hypotension, shock, or cardiac arrest with rapid IV use or overdose
Prolonged or complicated seizures (rare, typically in high-risk contexts)
Severe withdrawal syndrome (seizures, delirium, autonomic instability) after abrupt discontinuation
Worsening depression or emergence of suicidal thoughts in vulnerable individuals

safety.black_box_warning: Benzodiazepines, including diazepam, can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death when used with opioids. Use together only when alternatives are inadequate, at the lowest effective doses and shortest duration, with close monitoring.

contraindications.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity to diazepam or formulation components
Severe respiratory impairment (eg, significant COPD, severe sleep apnea)
Infants under 6 months of age for oral tablets

precautions: High risk of physical dependence and withdrawal; especially with higher doses, long duration, or frequent use.
Withdrawal can be severe and life-threatening (seizures, agitation, delirium) if stopped abruptly after prolonged use.
Abuse, misuse, and addiction risk is higher in people with a history of substance use disorders or concurrent use of other sedatives or alcohol.
Can cause drowsiness, impaired coordination, and slowed reaction time—major driving and fall risk.
Respiratory depression can occur, especially with comorbid lung disease, sleep apnea, or concurrent CNS depressants.
In older adults, associated with increased falls, fractures, cognitive decline, and mortality.
Paradoxical reactions (agitation, disinhibition, aggression) may occur, particularly in children, older adults, and people with certain psychiatric conditions.

interactions.interactant: Opioids (eg, oxycodone, hydrocodone, morphine, fentanyl, methadone)
interactions.mechanism: Black-box combination: high risk of profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death.
interactions.action: Avoid whenever possible. If absolutely necessary, use lowest effective doses for both, limit duration, and monitor closely for breathing problems.

interactions.mechanism: Markedly increased sedation, impaired coordination, and respiratory depression; higher overdose risk.
interactions.action: Avoid alcohol entirely while taking diazepam, especially during dose changes or high doses.

interactions.interactant: Other CNS depressants (eg, other benzodiazepines, barbiturates, Z-hypnotics, antipsychotics, sedating antidepressants, gabapentinoids, antihistamines)
interactions.mechanism: Additive or synergistic sedation, cognitive impairment, and fall risk.
interactions.action: Use with great caution or avoid; if combined, use the lowest effective doses with close monitoring.

interactions.interactant: CYP2C19/CYP3A4 inhibitors (eg, fluconazole, fluvoxamine, some SSRIs, azole antifungals, certain macrolides)
interactions.mechanism: May increase diazepam levels, prolonging effects and side effects.
interactions.action: Consider dose reduction and monitor for oversedation and cognitive impairment.

interactions.interactant: CYP inducers (eg, carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, St. John’s wort, chronic smoking for some pathways)
interactions.mechanism: May lower diazepam levels, reducing effectiveness.
interactions.action: Monitor for loss of effect; dose adjustments or alternative agents may be needed.

interactions.mechanism: Complex bidirectional interactions; potential changes in seizure threshold, sedation, and drug levels.
interactions.action: Coordinate with neurology; monitor seizures, side effects, and serum levels where appropriate.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Mental status, level of consciousness, and respiratory rate—especially with IV dosing or co-prescribed CNS depressants.
Blood pressure and heart rate, particularly during IV use and in older or medically fragile patients.
Signs of misuse or loss of control (early refills, escalating doses, combining with alcohol/other sedatives).
Fall risk, gait stability, and balance in older adults.
Liver function tests and CBC with long-term or high-dose therapy.
Withdrawal symptoms during tapering (anxiety, insomnia, tremor, perceptual disturbances, autonomic signs, seizures).
For seizure rescue use: frequency of seizure clusters, need for rescue doses, and adherence to limits (episodes per month).

special_populations.pregnancy: Diazepam crosses the placenta and can cause neonatal sedation and withdrawal. Teratogenic risk appears low but not zero. In some cases (eg, severe alcohol withdrawal or status epilepticus), benefits may outweigh risks. Use the lowest effective dose, involve obstetrics and psychiatry, and monitor newborns closely.
special_populations.lactation: Diazepam and active metabolites enter breast milk and have long half-lives in infants, especially newborns and preterm babies. This can cause infant sedation, poor feeding, weight loss, or withdrawal. In breastfeeding patients, shorter-acting benzodiazepines with simpler metabolism are generally preferred; if diazepam is used, use the lowest effective dose and monitor the infant carefully.
special_populations.pediatric: Rescue formulations (rectal gel, nasal spray, buccal film) are used for seizure clusters per weight-based protocols. For anxiety and muscle spasm, use is cautious and generally limited to short-term or specialized contexts. Avoid chronic daily therapy when possible.
special_populations.geriatric: Listed on Beers Criteria as potentially inappropriate due to high risk of falls, delirium, cognitive impairment, and prolonged sedation. If used, start at very low doses, titrate slowly, and reassess frequently. Avoid for insomnia or routine anxiety whenever possible.
special_populations.renal_impairment: No formal dose adjustment is required for isolated renal impairment, but accumulation of active metabolites and increased CNS effects can occur, especially with hypoalbuminemia and critical illness—use lower doses and monitor closely.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Diazepam clearance is significantly reduced in liver impairment, leading to prolonged half-life and accumulation. Avoid oral tablets in severe hepatic impairment and use reduced doses with close monitoring for milder liver disease.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed by oral and rectal routes; intranasal and buccal rescue products are rapidly absorbed for acute seizure treatment.
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: High oral, rectal, and intranasal bioavailability (~90% or greater for most routes).
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Oral: about 0.5–2.5 hours; rectal: ~1.5 hours; intranasal: ~1.5 hours; buccal: ~1 hour.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Parent diazepam typically 30–70 hours in adults, with even longer half-lives for active metabolites; elimination is significantly prolonged in older adults and hepatic impairment.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively hepatic; primarily via CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 to active metabolites (desmethyldiazepam, temazepam, oxazepam), which are further glucuronidated and renally excreted.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Primarily via urine as glucuronide conjugates of diazepam and metabolites.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: High-fat meals can delay and slightly reduce peak concentrations of oral diazepam but do not generally alter overall exposure.

dosing.titration: Diazepam dosing depends heavily on indication, age, organ function, and route. Below is a simplified overview for common psychiatry and behavioral health contexts. Always individualize and consult full prescribing information or local protocols.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Because diazepam is long-acting and can cause significant physical dependence, stopping must be done carefully.

sections.heading: What It’s Used For
sections.text: Diazepam is a versatile benzodiazepine used in both psychiatry and neurology, but because of its long half-life and dependence risk, it is reserved for specific situations rather than routine daily use for anxiety.
items: {link:condition:generalized-anxiety-disorder:Severe acute anxiety or agitation}: Short-term relief of intense anxiety or panic when fast calming is essential.
{link:condition:anxiety-disorders:Anxiety disorders (bridge treatment)}: Temporary use while first-line medications (like SSRIs/SNRIs) and psychotherapy start working.
{link:condition:alcohol-use-disorder:Alcohol withdrawal syndrome}: Reduces tremor, agitation, seizures, and delirium risk during withdrawal.
{link:condition:epilepsy:Seizure clusters (rescue therapy)}: Rectal, nasal, and buccal forms can stop intermittent seizure flurries.
{link:condition:status-epilepticus:Status epilepticus}: IV diazepam is an accepted emergency option when rapid seizure control is needed.
{link:condition:muscle-spasticity:Muscle spasm and spasticity}: Adjunctive treatment for muscle rigidity and spasms in certain neurologic conditions.
{link:condition:procedural-anxiety:Procedural anxiety and premedication}: Short-term use before procedures to reduce anxiety, provide sedation, and impair recall.
off_label: Adjunct in serotonin syndrome (for agitation and autonomic instability)
Adjunct in neuroleptic malignant syndrome (for rigidity and agitation)
Adjunct in stimulant intoxication (cocaine, methamphetamine) with severe agitation or hypertension
Adjunct for acute opioid withdrawal symptoms when preferred opioid agonists are not available and close monitoring is possible

sections.heading: What People Often Notice

quotes: My body and mind slowed down within about 30 minutes.
The shaking and sweating from withdrawal eased up after a few doses.
The seizure stopped and I slowly came back to myself.
items.note: When used appropriately, diazepam can quickly calm severe anxiety, withdrawal symptoms, or seizures.

quotes: It made me feel heavy and sleepy for much of the day.
My thinking felt slower and I had trouble concentrating.
I sometimes didn’t remember conversations from earlier.
items.note: Sleepiness, slowed thinking, and memory gaps are dose-related and more common with higher or repeated doses.

quotes: It worked so well that it was hard to stop.
When I cut down too fast, my anxiety and insomnia got much worse.
Missing doses suddenly made me feel shaky and wired.
items.note: The brain adapts to regular diazepam use. Stopping suddenly after sustained use can trigger withdrawal, which can be dangerous.

quotes: My parent seemed more confused and unsteady after starting it.
The falls got worse when they were on Valium regularly.
items.note: Older adults are very sensitive to sedation, confusion, and falls from long-acting benzodiazepines like diazepam.

sections.intro: People’s experiences with diazepam depend heavily on dose, route, and how often it is used.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Diazepam comes in several formulations used in different clinical situations. Some act very quickly for emergencies; others have slower onset.
key_points: IV: Works within 1–3 minutes for seizures or acute agitation.
Rectal gel: Typically acts within 2–10 minutes for seizure clusters.
Intranasal and buccal products: Designed for rapid rescue of seizures with onset over minutes.
Oral: Usually begins to reduce anxiety or muscle tension within 30–60 minutes.
Long half-life: Effects of repeated dosing can accumulate, leading to prolonged sedation and cognitive slowing, especially in older adults and those with liver disease.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Never combine diazepam with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives without clear medical supervision—this can slow breathing and may be fatal.
sections.black_box: Benzodiazepines, including diazepam, can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death when used with opioids. Use together only when alternatives are inadequate, at the lowest effective doses and shortest duration, with close monitoring.
other: High risk of physical dependence and withdrawal; especially with higher doses, long duration, or frequent use.
Withdrawal can be severe and life-threatening (seizures, agitation, delirium) if stopped abruptly after prolonged use.
Abuse, misuse, and addiction risk is higher in people with a history of substance use disorders or concurrent use of other sedatives or alcohol.
Can cause drowsiness, impaired coordination, and slowed reaction time—major driving and fall risk.
Respiratory depression can occur, especially with comorbid lung disease, sleep apnea, or concurrent CNS depressants.
In older adults, associated with increased falls, fractures, cognitive decline, and mortality.
Paradoxical reactions (agitation, disinhibition, aggression) may occur, particularly in children, older adults, and people with certain psychiatric conditions.
patient_counseling: Avoid alcohol, opioids, and other sedating drugs while taking diazepam unless specifically directed by your prescriber.
Do not drive, operate machinery, or do high-risk tasks until you know how diazepam affects you.
Use the smallest dose for the shortest time; this is not a maintenance medication for chronic anxiety in most people.
Never stop diazepam suddenly after regular use—work with your prescriber on a slow taper.
Tell your prescriber about any history of substance use problems, depression, or suicidal thoughts.
If you or your family notice confusion, severe drowsiness, trouble breathing, or unusual behavior, seek urgent medical help.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Diazepam’s most common side effects are sedation, dizziness, and impaired coordination. Long-term or high-dose use increases risks of cognitive problems, falls, and dependence.
plain_language_list: Slowed thinking, poor concentration, or memory gaps
Unsteady gait, poor coordination, and increased fall risk
Low blood pressure, especially when standing up quickly
Nausea, stomach discomfort, or changes in appetite
Changes in mood, including depression or emotional blunting

common.patient_note: Often strongest early in treatment or after dose increases; can impair driving and daily functioning.
Increases fall risk, particularly in older adults or those on other sedatives.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Because diazepam is long-acting and can cause significant physical dependence, stopping must be done carefully.
key_points: Never abruptly stop diazepam after weeks or months of regular use, unless there is a life-threatening reason.
Tapers are typically slower for long-acting benzodiazepines; reductions of 10–25% of the total daily dose every 1–2 weeks are common starting points, then slowed further near the end.
People with high doses, prolonged use, or a history of withdrawal complications may need very gradual tapers over months.
Monitor for rebound anxiety, insomnia, tremor, sensory changes, and, most importantly, seizures and confusion.
Non-benzodiazepine interventions (CBT, SSRIs/SNRIs, sleep hygiene, non-sedating medications) should be optimized during the taper to support successful discontinuation.

sections.heading: Dosing Information (Psychiatry-Focused Overview)
sections.text: Diazepam dosing depends heavily on indication, age, organ function, and route. Below is a simplified overview for common psychiatry and behavioral health contexts. Always individualize and consult full prescribing information or local protocols.

adult.alcohol_withdrawal: Typical regimens use 5–10 mg IV or PO as needed based on withdrawal scales (eg, CIWA-Ar), or fixed schedules (eg, 10 mg every 6 hours on day 1, then taper over several days) with additional PRN doses.
adult.severe_acute_anxiety_or_agitation: Often 2–10 mg PO, IV, or IM every 3–6 hours as needed, with careful limits on total daily dose and duration.
adult.anxiety_disorders_short_term: Commonly 2–5 mg orally once or twice daily, titrated cautiously up to a typical maximum of 40 mg/day in divided doses for very short-term use.
adult.procedural_premedication: Approximately 2–10 mg IV or PO as a single dose shortly before the procedure, titrated to effect and safety.
adult.seizure_clusters_rescue: Rectal, intranasal, or buccal weight-based fixed doses (eg, 0.2–0.5 mg/kg), usually limited to no more than 2 doses per episode, 1 episode every 5 days, and 5 episodes per month per product labeling.

sections.simple_explanation: For anxiety and alcohol withdrawal, diazepam is usually started at low doses and adjusted carefully for a short time. For seizure emergencies, specific weight-based rescue doses are used via rectal, nasal, or buccal routes and should follow a written seizure action plan.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: Diazepam requires particular caution in pregnancy, lactation, older adults, and patients with organ dysfunction or substance use disorders.
sections.pregnancy: Diazepam crosses the placenta and can cause neonatal sedation and withdrawal. Teratogenic risk appears low but not zero. In some cases (eg, severe alcohol withdrawal or status epilepticus), benefits may outweigh risks. Use the lowest effective dose, involve obstetrics and psychiatry, and monitor newborns closely.
sections.lactation: Diazepam and active metabolites enter breast milk and have long half-lives in infants, especially newborns and preterm babies. This can cause infant sedation, poor feeding, weight loss, or withdrawal. In breastfeeding patients, shorter-acting benzodiazepines with simpler metabolism are generally preferred; if diazepam is used, use the lowest effective dose and monitor the infant carefully.
sections.pediatrics: Rescue formulations (rectal gel, nasal spray, buccal film) are used for seizure clusters per weight-based protocols. For anxiety and muscle spasm, use is cautious and generally limited to short-term or specialized contexts. Avoid chronic daily therapy when possible.
sections.geriatrics: Listed on Beers Criteria as potentially inappropriate due to high risk of falls, delirium, cognitive impairment, and prolonged sedation. If used, start at very low doses, titrate slowly, and reassess frequently. Avoid for insomnia or routine anxiety whenever possible.
sections.hepatic: Diazepam clearance is significantly reduced in liver impairment, leading to prolonged half-life and accumulation. Avoid oral tablets in severe hepatic impairment and use reduced doses with close monitoring for milder liver disease.
sections.renal: No formal dose adjustment is required for isolated renal impairment, but accumulation of active metabolites and increased CNS effects can occur, especially with hypoalbuminemia and critical illness—use lower doses and monitor closely.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mental status, level of consciousness, and respiratory rate—especially with IV dosing or co-prescribed CNS depressants.
Blood pressure and heart rate, particularly during IV use and in older or medically fragile patients.
Signs of misuse or loss of control (early refills, escalating doses, combining with alcohol/other sedatives).
Fall risk, gait stability, and balance in older adults.
Liver function tests and CBC with long-term or high-dose therapy.
Withdrawal symptoms during tapering (anxiety, insomnia, tremor, perceptual disturbances, autonomic signs, seizures).
For seizure rescue use: frequency of seizure clusters, need for rescue doses, and adherence to limits (episodes per month).

sections.heading: Available Formulations (Psych-Relevant)
sections.text: Multiple formulations allow diazepam to be used in both planned and emergency situations.
items: Oral tablets: 2 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg (Valium and generics).
Oral solutions and concentrates (including Intensol 5 mg/mL) for flexible dosing.
Rectal gel (Diastat/Diastat AcuDial): weight-based single-use rescue for seizure clusters.
Intranasal solution (Valtoco): unit-dose nasal spray for seizure clusters in specific age/weight bands.
Buccal film (Libervant): weight-based film placed against the cheek for seizure rescue (approval status and availability may vary over time).
Injectable solution (IV/IM): 5 mg/mL for acute care and emergency settings.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Diazepam is a long-acting benzodiazepine that binds to benzodiazepine sites on GABA-A receptors in the brain. This increases the effect of GABA, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, allowing more chloride ions into neurons and stabilizing them in a less excitable state. The result is reduced anxiety, muscle relaxation, sedation, and a higher seizure threshold. It does not act on GABA-B receptors and has no antipsychotic or antidepressant effects.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In modern psychiatric practice, diazepam is not a first-line long-term treatment for anxiety disorders. It plays specific roles: as a short-term bridge in severe anxiety, as a key medication for alcohol withdrawal, and as a rescue agent for seizure clusters and status epilepticus. Because of its long half-life, strong dependence potential, and cognitive side effects, clinicians often prefer shorter-acting benzodiazepines or non-benzodiazepine strategies when possible. Chronic diazepam therapy requires careful risk–benefit review and slow, supervised tapers if deprescribing.

faqs.q: What is diazepam used for in mental health and neurology?
faqs.a: Diazepam is used short term for severe anxiety or agitation, to manage alcohol withdrawal symptoms, as an adjunct muscle relaxant for neurologic spasticity, and as a rescue medication for seizure clusters or status epilepticus. It is not usually a first-line long-term treatment for chronic anxiety disorders.

IV diazepam can work within 1–3 minutes in emergencies. Rectal gel, nasal spray, and buccal film for seizures usually work within minutes. Oral tablets typically begin to reduce anxiety or muscle tension in 30–60 minutes, but because diazepam is long-acting, sedation and other effects can last much longer.

Diazepam is a Schedule IV controlled substance with clear risk of abuse, misuse, and addiction. The risk increases with higher doses, longer duration, and history of substance use disorders. Physical dependence can develop even when used as prescribed, so long-term therapy must be carefully justified and monitored.

faqs.q: What are withdrawal symptoms if I stop diazepam too quickly?
faqs.a: Stopping diazepam abruptly after regular use can cause anxiety, insomnia, tremor, sweating, irritability, perceptual changes, and in severe cases, seizures, delirium, and autonomic instability. A gradual taper over weeks or months is usually needed to reduce these risks.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking diazepam?
faqs.a: No. Combining diazepam with alcohol significantly increases sedation, impairs coordination, and can suppress breathing. This combination is a major risk factor for overdose, falls, and accidents and should be avoided.

faqs.q: Why is diazepam considered risky in older adults?
faqs.a: Older adults clear diazepam more slowly, so the drug and its active metabolites can build up, causing prolonged sedation, confusion, memory problems, and increased fall and fracture risk. That is why most geriatric guidelines recommend avoiding long-acting benzodiazepines like diazepam whenever possible.

faqs.q: Is diazepam safe in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Diazepam can cross the placenta and enter breast milk. It may cause sedation and withdrawal in newborns and can accumulate in infants. In emergencies (like status epilepticus or severe alcohol withdrawal), benefits may outweigh risks, but for routine anxiety, other options are preferred. Decisions should be made with your obstetric and mental health providers.

faqs.q: What is the difference between diazepam and lorazepam?
faqs.a: Both are benzodiazepines, but diazepam is longer-acting and has active metabolites, leading to more accumulation, especially in older adults and liver disease. Lorazepam has a shorter half-life, no active metabolites, and is often preferred for certain acute situations and in liver impairment. Choice depends on indication, organ function, and duration of therapy.

faqs.q: How often can I use diazepam for seizure clusters?
faqs.a: Rescue products like rectal gel, intranasal spray, and buccal film typically limit use to no more than 1 treated seizure episode every 5 days and no more than 5 episodes per month. Your neurologist should provide a written seizure action plan with exact dose, route, and frequency limits.

faqs.q: Is diazepam an antidepressant or antipsychotic?
faqs.a: No. Diazepam can quickly relieve anxiety and agitation, but it does not treat the underlying biology of depression or psychosis. It is sometimes used briefly as an adjunct while primary treatments (like antidepressants or antipsychotics and psychotherapy) are started or adjusted.
